In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fatty acid composition of brain phospholipids in formula- and human milk-fed piglets is not predictable from the composition of their plasma phospholipidis, and that the fatty acid compositions of liver and bile phospholipids are only weakly related to the fatty acid compositions in plasma phospholiptids.
plasma phospholipd fatty acids are not a reliable indicator of diet-related differences in brain fatty acids, but may provide a reasonable estimate of differences in liver and bile fatty acids.
analysis of fatty acids in plasma phospholipoproteins may be useful to predict diet-induced differences in liver and bile fatty acids but not brain fatty acid composition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
analysis of plasma phosphatidylcholine fatty acids is a good predictor of liver and bile fatty acid composition, but is less useful for brain.

analysis of plasma phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin fatty acids can provide information on the fatty acid composition of bile, but not liver or brain, and that analysis of plasma fatty acids may be a useful tool for monitoring the effect of formula composition on the fatty acid status of the liver.

plasma phospholipd fatty acids are useful for predicting changes in the proportions of saturated and (n-6), but not (n-3), fatty acids in liver phospholipids, and for predicting changes in all major fatty acids in bile, but only saturated fatty acids in brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plasma phospholipipid fatty acids may be used to predict diet-induced differences in liver and bile fatty acids, but not necessarily brain fatty acids.
analysis of plasma phospho-lipid fatty acids can be used to predict changes in liver and possibly bile fatty acids in infants fed formula or human milk.
analysis of plasma phosphatidylcholine fatty acids is not likely to be a useful method of determining diet-related changes in brain fatty acids in infants.
